docs.title: Course Information
docs.text:
The Computing Technology course, first introduced in 2024, represents a significant update to the curriculum, which had remained unchanged since 2003. This transformation brings a contemporary perspective to computing education, addressing the substantial evolution in the field over two decades. Students and educators are fortunate to engage with this modern syllabus, given that computing in 2003 would appear drastically different and outdated today.

However, it's important to recognize that even as the syllabus was being finalized around 2022, the landscape of computing was rapidly shifting. Notably, advancements in generative AI, which were less developed and not widely utilized until the end of 2022, highlight the fast-paced nature of technological change. This context underscores the need for continuous adaptation and learning within the field of computing.

docs.title: Directly from the Syllabus:
docs.text:
Studying Computing Technology 7–10 enables students to develop skills in the specific application of computing technologies and to develop digital solutions applicable to a range of industrial, commercial and recreational contexts.

Computing Technology 7–10 focuses on computational, design and systems thinking. It also develops data analysis and programming (coding) skills. The knowledge and skills developed in the course enable students to contribute to an increasingly technology-focused world.

When studying Computing Technology 7–10, students have opportunities to develop skills in analysing data, designing for user experience, connecting people and systems, developing websites and apps, building mechatronic systems, and creating simulations or games. Students use hardware and software to manage and secure data. They also investigate the social, ethical and legal responsibilities of using data as creators of digital solutions while considering privacy and cybersecurity principles.

Students engage with contemporary and advancing technologies that improve access and participation in society. Students explore the impact of innovations in computing technology on society and the environment. They develop skills using a range of hardware and software applications, including multimedia, digital media, virtual and augmented realities, gaming, graphical data and visualisations, networks and devices.

The Computing Technology 7–10 Syllabus builds on the knowledge and skills developed in the Digital Technologies context in the Technology 7–8 Syllabus. Students advance their computing skills across technical knowledge, social and cultural awareness, project management and thinking skills. They are able to transfer knowledge to new situations, building on technical skills and experiences. Students improve their project-management skills through planning, collaboration, communicating ideas, engaging in processes and designing solutions.

Students become increasingly confident, creative, efficient and discerning when using and developing a range of digital products/solutions. They expand their understanding of related work environments while developing skills to equip them for further education, vocational pathways and personal interests.

docs.title: Algorithms
docs.text:
It is expected that students are able to develop and interpret algorithms represented as pseudocode and flowcharts.

Algorithms are built on three main concepts:

Sequence

This is the main processes of your program. Setting variables, running linear routines, making calculations, basic output. User cannot make choices or really interact with the system much at all here.

Branching / Selection

This is where the program makes decisions - think user input and IF statements. This is where the user can begin to influence the program, as the program will make decisions based on input.

Iteration / Repetition

This is where we get to loops to keep certain routines running. A program may keep running until it exits, or certain processes may run until a user does something specific.

Now in terms of our programs, to keep everything efficient in Python we create a main() function then reference various other functions in main(). When considering algorithms, we call this a mainline and subroutines.

Subroutines / Functions

A subroutine is essentially a function which is called into the mainline. The algorithm for the subroutine is referenced in the mainline, but is actually created separately. This is similar to how a Python function can be used in the main() function, but is created in a different area.

This helps to keep our algorithms efficient, readable and useable.

It is important to start complex algorithms with a clear, uncluttered mainline. The mainline should reference required subroutines, the details of which are shown in separate algorithms.

Each subroutine should be concise and correctly make use of further subroutines for detailed logic.

docs.text:
Before we move into learning data analysis, first we need to understand what information systems are used for and why, as well as the implications of using them.

There is no point in applying what you have learned about computer programming if you do not understand what a computer is for.

This will take around two weeks and will both teach you the basics of computing, and how to structure a paragraph for a short-answer response.

As you complete the work, you will need to write down definitions of key terms from your teacher's presentation and complete set questions each lesson. You will be provided with teacher presentations and textbook notes.

We will also be using two external Python libraries - Pandas and Matplotlib.

docs.title: What is Pandas?
docs.text: Pandas is a Python library used for data manipulation and analysis. It provides two main data structures — Series (for one-dimensional data) and DataFrame (for two-dimensional tabular data) — making it easy to clean, filter, group, and analyze data efficiently.

docs.title: What is Matplotlib?
docs.text: Matplotlib is a plotting library for Python that allows you to create static, animated, and interactive visualisations. It's commonly used to generate charts like line graphs, bar charts, and histograms to help interpret and present data visually.

docs.title: We Live in a Data-Driven Society
docs.text:
Our society is increasingly being driven by big data and large-scale data analysis. From personalised recommendations on platforms like Netflix and Spotify to predictive algorithms used in online shopping and targeted advertising, data is shaping the way we consume content and products. In healthcare, large datasets are analysed to track disease outbreaks, improve diagnosis, and develop more effective treatments.

Governments use big data for urban planning and traffic management, while financial institutions rely on it to detect fraud and assess credit risk. In sports, data analytics is used to improve athlete performance and game strategy. Even the way in which we educate and assess here at Gosford High School is influenced by data analysis.

docs.title: Data Science is Useful in ALL Industries
docs.text:
Learning data science with Python isn’t just for tech careers—it’s useful in almost every field. Whether you’re interested in sports, business, healthcare, fashion, or even music, data is everywhere. Coaches use it to improve team performance, businesses use it to understand customers, and doctors use it to track health trends.

In many science degrees today, students have to learn to use Python, Pandas and Matplotlib (which we WILL be learning in this unit).

docs.title: Algorithms
docs.text:
It is expected that you are able to develop and interpret algorithms represented as pseudocode and flowcharts.

Algorithms are built on three main concepts:

Sequence

This is the main processes of your program. Setting variables, running linear routines, making calculations, basic output. User cannot make choices or really interact with the system much at all here.

Branching / Selection

This is where the program makes decisions - think user input and IF statements. This is where the user can begin to influence the program, as the program will make decisions based on input.

Iteration / Repetition

This is where we get to loops to keep certain routines running. A program may keep running until it exits, or certain processes may run until a user does something specific.

Now in terms of our programs, to keep everything efficient in Python we create a main() function then reference various other functions in main(). When considering algorithms, we call this a mainline and subroutines.

Subroutines / Functions

A subroutine is essentially a function which is called into the mainline. The algorithm for the subroutine is referenced in the mainline, but is actually created separately. This is similar to how a Python function can be used in the main() function, but is created in a different area.

This helps to keep our algorithms efficient, readable and useable.

It is important to start complex algorithms with a clear, uncluttered mainline. The mainline should reference required subroutines, the details of which are shown in separate algorithms.

Each subroutine should be concise and correctly make use of further subroutines for detailed logic.

docs.title: Directional Verbs
docs.text:
When responding to a question in any task at school, it is important to consider how to answer the question. Instead of just filling a box with as much Google gobbledygook, waffling and repetitive drivel, you need to address what the question is actually asking you.

The best way to do this is to look for the directional verb.

docs.title: What is that?
docs.text:
The directional verb, normally at the beginning of a question (or a sentence if the question is multiple sentences), tells you how you need to frame your answer. For instance, consider the following:

Info

Explain how data privacy is maintained and what measures are in place to protect user information.

In the above, the directional verb is explain. NESA (accreditation body for schools in NSW) has a glossary of key words, which defines "explain" as:

  • Relate cause and effect.
  • Make the relationships between things evident.
  • Provide why and/or how.

This means that when the above question asks you to explain how data privacy is maintained, you not only need to describe data privacy principles, but need to explain how privacy is maintained and make the relationship between data privacy maintenance and the measures in place clear.

In short, consider HOW and/or WHY something is the case, and make connections between HOW / WHY and the WHAT.

docs.title: Another Example
docs.text:
Info

Describe the mechatronic system’s components, including:

  • Inputs (sensors and data sources)
  • Storage methods
  • Transmission processes
  • Processing units
  • Actuators and outputs

In the above, the directional verb is describe. NESA's glossary of key words defines "describe" as:

  • Provide characteristics and features.

This means that in the above, whilst you need to describe WHAT the mechatronic system's components are, WHAT purpose they serve and provide information about their features, you do not need to explain how or why they are used.

docs.title: Working Collaboratively
docs.text:
Collaboration is essential when completing a task as it allows individuals to share ideas, divide workload efficiently, and build a more comprehensive understanding of the topic. Working together enables group members to bring different perspectives and expertise, leading to more well-rounded conclusions. It also helps develop important skills such as communication, problem-solving, and adaptability—skills that are highly valued in both academic and professional settings.

Additionally, collaboration fosters accountability and time management, as team members rely on each other to contribute effectively. By working together, challenges can be addressed more efficiently, and feedback can be given to refine ideas and improve the quality of the work. Ultimately, teamwork enhances learning by creating an environment where knowledge is constructed collectively, leading to stronger outcomes than working alone.

docs.title: Development
docs.text: Typically when we develop software, we may start by working on the mainline algorithm, then creating the subroutines separately. This allows us to work on our main flow and functions separately.

docs.title: Decomposition
docs.text:
Decomposition in software design is the process of breaking down a complex system into smaller, more manageable components. Let's take a text-based adventure game for example. Developing our mainline algorithm in main.py and our subroutines in a different module such as actions.py allows us to narrow our focus on different elements of the project.

main.py would include the main user interface and may be developed first. The first rendition may look something like the following:

main.py
def main():
    print("Welcome to the Adventure Game!")
    print("A wild creature appears! What do you do?")
    print("1. Fight")
    print("2. Run away")

    choice = input("Enter your choice (1, 2, or 3): ")

    if choice == "1":
        print('Fight function Here')
    elif choice == "2":
        print('Run away function here')
    else:
        print("Invalid choice. Please restart and pick a valid option.")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

The above sets out how the UI will function, but so far only demonstrates that the user interface works.

Now, let's look at another module, actions.py, where we'll put the functions.

actions.py
def fight():
    """
    Function to handle the fight action.
    This could include various logic for fighting a creature.
    """
    print("You chose to fight the creature!")
    # Add more fight logic here as needed
    print("You engage in battle with the creature.")
    # Example of more details
    print("The creature is strong, but you're stronger!")

def run_away():
    """
    Function to handle the run away action.
    This could include logic for successfully running away or failing to escape.
    """
    print("You chose to run away!")
    # Add more run away logic here as needed
    print("You turn and flee from the creature.")
    # Example of a scenario where running away fails
    print("Unfortunately, the creature is too fast! It catches up with you!")

The beauty of this is that in the above, we can test the run_away and fight functions in the actions.py module prior to using them in the main user interface, and we can test the user interface thoroughly without needing to run through all the functions.

docs.title: Integration
docs.text:
Whilst your program is unlikely to require this step, it is an important step in the process of software development.

Once we have developed our mainline routine (main.py) and our subroutines (actions.py), we need to bring the subroutine into the main routine. We also need to ensure both files are in the same folder.

So let's see an example of integration into our main.py file now:

main.py
# We could also just type "import actions" to get all functions
# "from actions import *" to get all functions as well
from actions import fight, run_away 

def main():
    print("A wild creature appears! What do you do?")
    print("1. Fight")
    print("2. Run away")

    choice = input("Enter your choice (1, 2, or 3): ")

    if choice == "1":
        fight()  # Calls the fight function from actions.py
    elif choice == "2":
        run_away()  # Calls the run_away function from actions.py
    else:
        print("Invalid choice. Please restart and pick a valid option.")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

docs.title: Comments vs Docstrings
docs.text:
Comments and docstrings are both ways to add explanatory text to your code, but they serve different purposes and have different formatting conventions. Here's a breakdown of their comparison and contrast:

Comments
  • Structure: Comments can be single-line (// in C++, # in Python) or multi-line (/* ... */ in C++) depending on the programming language. They are typically placed within the code block they are explaining.
  • Use: Comments are used to explain specific lines of code, algorithms, or logic choices made by the programmer. They can also be used for temporary notes or reminders to be removed later such as #TODO
Docstrings
  • Structure: Docstrings are multi-line strings (usually placed at the beginning of a class, function, or module) that follow specific formatting conventions depending on the language. They use special delimiters like triple quotes (""" ... """) in Python.
  • Use: Docstrings provide comprehensive explanations for classes, functions, or modules. They typically cover the purpose, usage, parameters, return values, and sometimes even examples. They are meant to be permanent documentation for anyone using the code.

We can also check what a function does, by asking it. This helps maintainability.

def my_function:
"""This is a docstring for MyClass"""
pass

# Print the docstring of MyClass

help(my_function)
print(my_function.__doc__)
Feature Comments Docstrings Purpose Explain specific code sections Document classes, functions, or modules Placement Within the code block being explained At the beginning of the definition Formatting Language-dependent (usually single or multi-line) Language-specific formatting conventions (e.g., triple quotes in Python) Permanence Can be temporary (for notes/reminders) Meant to be permanent documentation Level of Detail Brief explanations Comprehensive descriptions

docs.title: When Should I use a Comment or DocString?
docs.text:
• Use comments to explain "why" you wrote a specific piece of code.
  • Use docstrings to document "what" a class, function, or module does and "how" to use it.
def create_historic_character(name, era):
    """Create a historical character with a name and era.

    Args:
        name (str): The character's name.
        era (str): The historical era.

    Returns:
        str: A formatted description of the character.
    """
    return f"{name} lived during the {era}."

# Example usage
print(create_historic_character("Leonardo da Vinci", "Renaissance"))

The docstring provides an explanation of the function and what it does:

  • Function Purpose: To create a historical character with a name and era.
  • Arguments: It defines a section titled "Args" that explains each argument taken by the function:
  • name: The name of the historical figure.
  • era: The historical era the figure belongs to.
  • Returns: Outlines the that a description of the character is returned from the function.

This docstring improves code readability and maintainability by providing clear explanations for anyone using the create_historic_character function.

I can outline the lifestyle and societal challenges which need to be considered when designing video games.

Game developers need to consider more than whether a game works technically. The decisions made during development can affect players, other people and society. Developers therefore need to consider ethical, social and legal issues when deciding what a game should contain, what information it should collect and how players should interact with it.

docs.title: Ethical issues
docs.text:
Ethical issues concern questions about what is responsible, fair or right. A game may technically be capable of doing something without that automatically meaning that it should do it.

For example, a developer could design a system that gives players increasingly valuable rewards when they continue playing for long periods. The developer should consider whether the design is encouraging healthy engagement or deliberately attempting to keep players playing for longer than they intended.

Fairness is another ethical consideration. If players compete against each other, developers need to think about whether the rules provide a reasonable opportunity for players to succeed. A game that gives certain players significant advantages because they have paid additional money may raise questions about fairness, particularly if the game presents itself as a competitive experience.

docs.title: Social issues
docs.text:
Social issues concern the effects that a game can have on individuals and groups. Online games can provide opportunities for cooperation and communication, but they can also expose players to bullying, harassment and inappropriate behaviour.

Developers can respond through features such as:

  • Reporting
  • Blocking
  • Moderation
  • Restrictions on communication

Games can also influence social attitudes through the characters, cultures and groups they represent, so developers should consider whether their representations reinforce harmful stereotypes or exclude particular groups.

docs.title: Legal issues
docs.text:
Legal issues are concerned with requirements established by law.

Copyright is particularly relevant to game development because games contain many creative works, including:

  • Artwork
  • Music
  • Photographs
  • Sound effects
  • Software code

Developers cannot simply assume that material found online is free to copy. They need to understand ownership, licensing and permission before using another person's work.

docs.title: Privacy
docs.text:
Privacy is another important legal and ethical consideration. Games may collect information such as account details, gameplay information or other personal data.

Developers need to consider:

  • Why the information is being collected
  • Whether it is necessary
  • How it will be protected
  • What users should be told about its collection and use

Collecting information simply because it is technically possible may not be appropriate.

docs.title: Responding to scenarios
docs.text:
When responding to an ethical, social or legal scenario, students should move beyond simply naming the issue. A strong response identifies the issue, explains its potential impact and explains why the developer should be concerned about it.

For example, if a game collects unnecessary personal information:

  • The issue is privacy.
  • The impact could be increased risk to players if the information is exposed or misused.
  • The developer should therefore minimise unnecessary data collection and protect information appropriately.

These issues often overlap.

A decision can be legal but still raise ethical questions, or a design decision can have both social and ethical consequences.

The important skill is to apply the concept to the particular game scenario rather than simply listing a definition.

docs.title: Game Design and Requirements
docs.text:
Learning Intention

Specify the functional requirements of a game or simulation, including stating the purpose of a system, describing use cases and developing test cases of inputs and expected outputs

Specify the non-functional requirements of a game or simulation

Success Criteria

I can distinguish between functional and non-functional requirements of video games.

I can specify functional and non-functional requirements of a video game in a given scenario.

Before a game is developed, the development team needs to understand what the game is expected to do and what constraints it must operate under. These expectations are called requirements. Requirements provide a clear description of what the client and users need from the finished product. Without clear requirements, different people involved in a project can make different assumptions about what the game should contain.

docs.title: Functional Requirements
docs.text:
A functional requirement describes something the game must do. Functional requirements are concerned with features, actions and behaviour.

For example, a game might need to allow a player to:

  • Create a profile
  • Select a mission
  • Customise a vehicle
  • Save progress
  • Compete against another player

Each of these describes behaviour that the software must provide.

A useful way to identify a functional requirement is to ask:

What does the system need to do?

docs.title: Non-Functional Requirements
docs.text:
A non-functional requirement describes a quality, constraint or condition that the game must satisfy. It is not usually describing a new feature; instead, it describes how the system should operate or a limitation under which it must operate.

A game might need to:

  • Load a level within a particular amount of time
  • Operate on a specified type of device
  • Protect player information
  • Remain usable for people with particular accessibility needs
  • Maintain an acceptable level of performance

A useful question for identifying a non-functional requirement is:

How well does it need to work, or what restriction does it need to meet?

docs.title: Understanding the Difference
docs.text:
The distinction can sometimes be subtle.

  • “Players can change the difficulty level” is functional because it describes something the game allows the player to do.
  • “The difficulty setting must be accessible from the main menu” describes a usability requirement.
  • “The game saves the player's progress” is functional.
  • “The game must save progress without noticeable delay” is non-functional.

docs.title: Identifying Requirements in a Client Brief
docs.text:
A client brief often contains requirements without explicitly labelling them. Students therefore need to read the scenario carefully and identify the needs hidden within it.

They should consider:

  • Who the users are
  • What those users need to accomplish
  • Where the game will be used
  • What platform it will run on
  • What restrictions or expectations the client has

Age, audience, hardware, accessibility, performance, privacy and budget can all influence the design.

docs.title: Writing Clear Requirements
docs.text:
Requirements should be specific enough that developers can make decisions about whether they have actually been met.

Make Requirements Clear

“The game should be easy to use” is difficult to measure because different people may have different ideas about what “easy” means.

A more useful requirement might specify that a new player should be able to begin a game without assistance after completing a short tutorial.

Clear requirements reduce misunderstandings between the client and development team and give developers something against which the completed system can be evaluated.

docs.title: User Interface and Controls
docs.text:
Learning Intention

Describe inputs, storage, transmission, processes and outputs in games and/or simulations

Explore design principles and issues relevant to game design

Evaluate an existing game or simulation in terms of its mechanics, aesthetics and usability

Success Criteria

I can identify and explain design principles and issues relevant to specific game design scenarios.

I can evaluate games in given scenarios in terms of mechanics, aesthetics and/or usability.

I can consider the appropriateness of an input setup for the intended audience.

The user interface, or UI, is the part of a game through which the player interacts with the software and receives information from it. This includes menus, buttons, icons, maps, status displays, inventories, instructions, and the controls used to operate the game.

A good user interface allows players to understand what is happening and what they can do without unnecessary confusion.

docs.title: Usability
docs.text:
Usability is an important part of interface design. A usable interface is relatively easy to learn, predictable, and consistent. Players should be able to understand the purpose of controls and find important information without having to search unnecessarily.

Consistency is particularly important in games. If a particular button performs an action in one part of a game, changing its function without a good reason can make the game confusing.

docs.title: Feedback
docs.text:
Feedback is another important part of usability. When a player performs an action, the game should normally provide some indication of what happened.

If a player selects an option, the interface might:

  • Change appearance
  • Display a message
  • Play a sound

If an action cannot be performed, the game should provide an understandable explanation rather than simply ignoring the player's input. Good feedback helps players build an understanding of how the game works.

docs.title: Accessibility
docs.text:
Accessibility means designing the game so that people with different abilities can use it. Accessibility is not simply about making a game easier. It involves removing unnecessary barriers that could prevent someone from accessing the game's content or controls.

For example:

  • Important information should not be communicated through colour alone because some players may have difficulty distinguishing particular colours.
  • Subtitles can provide access to spoken information for players who cannot hear it clearly.
  • Adjustable text size can assist players who have difficulty reading small text.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
Controls should be appropriate for the intended audience and platform.

  • A touchscreen game may need large, clearly separated touch controls.
  • A keyboard-and-mouse game can use different input methods.
  • Some players may benefit from being able to remap controls, adjust sensitivity, or choose alternative ways of performing an action.

The best control scheme is not necessarily the one with the most features; it is the one that allows the intended users to interact with the game effectively.

docs.title: Balancing Appearance and Usability
docs.text:
An engaging interface can make a game more enjoyable, but visual appearance should not take priority over usability. An interface can contain impressive graphics and animations while still being difficult to understand.

Effective game design balances appearance, feedback, consistency, accessibility, and ease of use. Developers should consider the needs of the intended audience rather than assuming that every player will interact with the game in the same way.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:

A. Copyright\ B. Privacy\ C. Cyberbullying\ D. Accessibility

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:

  • Players can purchase items that provide advantages over other players.

Identify whether each issue is primarily social, ethical or legal.

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:

docs.title: Question 5
docs.text:
Stimulus

A game development company is creating an online adventure game aimed at students aged 13–16. Players explore a large virtual world, complete missions and compete against other players.

The game will be free to download, but players will be able to purchase cosmetic items such as character outfits and accessories. Some items will only be available for a limited time, and players will receive notifications when these items are about to disappear from the store.

The game will also include an online communication system that allows players to send messages to other players. The development team has proposed automatically recording messages that are reported by players so they can be reviewed by moderators. Players will be able to block other users, but the development team has not yet decided whether players should be able to use the game without providing personal information.

The company plans to collect information about how players use the game so that it can recommend content and display advertisements that are more relevant to individual players. The company believes that collecting more information will allow it to improve the game and increase its revenue.

Some members of the development team have raised concerns about the impact of the game on younger players. They are particularly concerned about players feeling pressured to make purchases, spending excessive amounts of time playing, being exposed to inappropriate communication, and having their personal information collected.

Question

Discuss the social, ethical and legal issues that the development team should consider before releasing the game.

In your response, refer to specific features of the proposed game and explain the possible implications of these features for players and the development company.

docs.title: Context Diagrams
docs.text:
Learning Intention

Use program-development support tools, including Input Process Output (IPO) charts/diagrams, decision trees, flowcharts and structured English/pseudocode, in the development of a game or simulation

Develop appropriate supporting documentation in a program to ensure it is easy to read, understand and maintain

Create a record of project development demonstrating iterative design and evaluation

Success Criteria

I can plan and represent the overarching flow of a system using a context diagram.

I can identify and use the correct symbols to represent data flows, systems and external entities.

A context diagram, also called a Level 0 Data Flow Diagram (DFD), provides a high-level view of a system. It represents the entire system as a single process and shows how data moves between the system and the external entities that interact with it.

A context diagram does not show the individual processes or data stores within the system. Instead, it focuses on the system boundary and identifies what data enters and leaves the system.

For example, a game might have a Player as an external entity. The player could send data such as “Login Details” or “Game Input” to the game system, while the game system could send data such as “Game Display” or “Game Results” back to the player.

A context diagram therefore answers the question:

“What data enters and leaves the system, and who or what does it interact with?”

docs.title: How to Construct
docs.text: The following symbols are used to construct data flow diagrams, however, a context diagram does not use any data stores.

docs.title: Voting System Example
docs.text: In the following system, candidates put their details into the voting system. Voters put in details and vote using the voting system, and receive a confirmation that they have voted. The voting system then generates election results to output to the public.

docs.title: Video Game Example
docs.text:
The following is a video game requiring a login and connects to an online service.

The player could send data such as “Login Details” or “Game Input” to the game system, while the game system could send data such as “Game Display” or “Game Results” back to the player.

An online service may send palyer data to the game system, and the game system will share game data with the online service.

A context diagram is useful as the starting point for developing a more detailed DFD. The Level 1 DFD expands the single process from the context diagram into the major processes within the system and can also show data stores. The external entities and major data flows shown in the context diagram should remain consistent when the system is expanded into the Level 1 DFD.

docs.title: Data Flow Diagrams
docs.text:
Learning Intention

Use program-development support tools, including Input Process Output (IPO) charts/diagrams, decision trees, flowcharts and structured English/pseudocode, in the development of a game or simulation

Develop appropriate supporting documentation in a program to ensure it is easy to read, understand and maintain

Create a record of project development demonstrating iterative design and evaluation

Success Criteria

I can plan and represent a range of processes and data flows using a data flow diagram (Level 1).

I can identify and use the correct symbols to represent data flows, data stores, processes and external entities.

A Data Flow Diagram (DFD) is a way of representing how data moves through a system. In a game, a DFD can be used to show where information comes from, what the game does with that information, where information is stored, and where information is sent.

A DFD is concerned with the movement and handling of data rather than the order in which instructions are carried out. For example, a game might receive information about a player's selected character, use that information to load the character's attributes, and then send the resulting character information to the gameplay system.

A Level 1 DFD provides more detail about the major processes within a system.

docs.title: Main components
docs.text: The four main components you need to recognise are external entities, processes, data stores and data flows.

docs.title: External entities
docs.text:
An external entity is something outside the system that provides data to the system or receives data from it.

In a game, a player, an online service or a game administrator could be an external entity. The entity is considered external because it interacts with the software but is not itself part of the software being represented.

docs.title: Processes
docs.text:
A process represents something the system does with data. It receives information, uses or changes that information, and produces a result.

Processes should normally describe an action, such as:

  • “Validate Player Profile”
  • “Calculate Race Result”
  • “Update Mission”

A process is different from a piece of data. “Player Profile” describes information, whereas “Load Player Profile” describes an operation performed by the system.

docs.title: Data stores
docs.text:
A data store represents information that the system keeps so that it can be used later.

A game might store:

  • Player profiles
  • Saved progress
  • Unlocked achievements
  • Tournament results

The important idea is that a data store represents persistent information rather than an action being performed by the program. Data can be sent to a data store when information is saved and retrieved from it when information is needed.

docs.title: Data flows
docs.text:
A data flow represents data moving between components of the system.

The direction of the flow is important because it indicates where the data is coming from and where it is going. For example, a player might provide “Character Selection” to a process that loads the chosen character. The arrow represents the movement of that information, not simply the fact that two components are related.

docs.title: Video Game Example
docs.text:
The following is a video game requiring a login and allows the player to save their game progress.

The player sends Login Details to the Manage Player process, which accesses Player Data stored in the Player Data data store. The player also sends Game Input to the Manage Gameplay process, which uses the player data to produce Game Display and Game Results for the player.

When the player makes progress, Game Progress is sent to Save Game, which stores the information in the Saved Games data store. Saved game data can also be retrieved and sent back to Manage Gameplay when the player loads a saved game.

docs.title: Interpreting a DFD
docs.text:
When interpreting a DFD, you should carefully consider what each element represents and whether the direction of each data flow makes sense.

Common Mistake

A common mistake is to treat an action as though it were data. “Open Inventory” is an action, while “Inventory Request” or “Inventory Data” describes information that could appropriately be represented as a data flow.

You should also be able to distinguish between a process that handles information and a data store that retains information.

docs.title: Why DFDs are useful
docs.text:
DFDs are useful because they allow a developer to understand how information moves through a system before considering the detailed code.

They can reveal:

  • Missing data flows
  • Incorrect directions
  • Unnecessary processes
  • Places where information needs to be stored

A DFD therefore provides a model of the information requirements of a game rather than a model of the game's user interface or program structure.

docs.title: Decision Trees
docs.text:
Learning Intention

Use program-development support tools, including Input Process Output (IPO) charts/diagrams, decision trees, flowcharts and structured English/pseudocode, in the development of a game or simulation

Create and modify algorithms and code that use branching and iteration, and represent them diagrammatically and in English

Develop appropriate supporting documentation in a program to ensure it is easy to read, understand and maintain

Create a record of project development demonstrating iterative design and evaluation

Success Criteria

I can plan and represent decisions in a game system using a decision tree

I can represent decision making in a range of game design scenarios.

A decision tree is a representation of decisions made by a system. It begins with a question or condition and branches into different possible paths depending on the result. Each path eventually leads to an outcome. Decision trees are useful in games because many gameplay systems need to respond differently depending on the current situation.

A decision in a game is normally based on a condition that can be evaluated. For example, a game might need to determine whether a player has completed a mission, whether an item is available, whether a character has enough energy to perform an action, or whether an enemy is within a particular distance. The condition produces different possible outcomes, which are represented as branches.

Consider a game in which a player approaches a locked research facility. The game might first check whether the player has the access card. If they do, the game could then check whether the facility's security system is active. Depending on the answers, the player might be allowed inside, required to disable the security system, or prevented from entering. A decision tree makes these different paths visible and allows the developer to check whether every possible situation has been considered.

The branches of a decision tree represent the possible results of a decision. For a simple condition, these might be "Yes" and "No", although more than two outcomes are possible. The final result of following a series of branches is an outcome. An outcome might be an action performed by the game, a message displayed to the player, a change to the game state or another decision that needs to be evaluated.

Decision trees are particularly useful for planning game logic because they make complex choices easier to see. Without a clear representation, developers can accidentally forget an outcome or create contradictory conditions. By following each branch from the beginning to an outcome, the developer can test whether the logic accounts for all relevant situations.

Decision trees can also be translated into pseudocode. A branch asking whether a player has enough energy could become an IF statement. If the condition is true, the program performs one action; otherwise, it performs another. For example, if a player has enough energy, the game could allow a special move; otherwise, it could display a message explaining that the move cannot currently be performed.

When creating a decision tree, you should make sure that:

  • Each decision is actually a question or condition.
  • The branches represent possible answers.
  • The outcomes clearly describe what the system does next.
  • The decision tree represents the logic of the system rather than simply listing a series of unrelated actions.

docs.title: IPO Charts
docs.text:
Learning Intention

Use program-development support tools, including Input Process Output (IPO) charts/diagrams, decision trees, flowcharts and structured English/pseudocode, in the development of a game or simulation

Develop appropriate supporting documentation in a program to ensure it is easy to read, understand and maintain

Create a record of project development demonstrating iterative design and evaluation

Success Criteria

I can develop IPO charts to plan a particular process in a game design scenario.

I can correctly identify inputs, processes and outputs in a game design scenario.

An IPO chart describes a process using three stages: Input, Process and Output. It is useful for identifying what information a particular part of a program receives, what the program does with that information, and what result it produces. IPO charts are commonly used during system design because they provide a simple way of planning a process before writing code.

docs.title: Input
docs.text:
An input is information provided to the process. In a game, an input could be a player's button press, a selected option, a value retrieved from a data store, or information about an object in the game world.

The important point is that the input is information being provided to the process, rather than simply the physical device that produced it. For example, when a player presses a controller button, the relevant input to the software is the button press or command.

docs.title: Process
docs.text:
The process describes what the system does with the input. This might involve calculations, comparisons, searches, updates or decisions.

For example, a game could receive a player's selected character and then check that character's available abilities. The processing is the work the software performs to turn the input into a result.

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
The output is the information or result produced by the process. An output could be an updated score, a message, a new position, a changed game state or information displayed to the player.

An output does not have to be something displayed on the screen. It could also be information sent to another part of the program or saved for later use.

docs.title: Example: Purchasing an Item in a Game
docs.text:
Consider a game that allows a player to purchase an item:

Input Process Output Item selected Check the item's price against the player's available coins Updated inventory Player's current number of coins If the purchase is valid, update the player's inventory and coin total

New coin total

Message confirming the purchase

docs.title: Using IPO Charts
docs.text:
IPO charts are useful because they encourage developers to think about the boundaries of a process. You should be able to distinguish between an input and the device used to provide it, and between an output and the device used to display or produce it.

For example:

  • A keyboard is an input device, but "player presses the W key" is an input to a movement process.
  • A monitor is an output device, but "updated player position displayed" is an output.

IPO charts also connect closely to programming. Once the inputs, processing and outputs have been identified, the processing can be translated into pseudocode or program code. This makes the IPO chart a useful planning tool rather than simply a diagram to complete after the program has already been designed.

docs.title: Structure Charts
docs.text:
Learning Intention

Use program-development support tools, including Input Process Output (IPO) charts/diagrams, decision trees, flowcharts and structured English/pseudocode, in the development of a game or simulation

Create and modify algorithms and code that use branching and iteration, and represent them diagrammatically and in English

Develop appropriate supporting documentation in a program to ensure it is easy to read, understand and maintain

Create a record of project development demonstrating iterative design and evaluation

Success Criteria

I can plan and represent system modules / functions using a structure chart.

I can identify and use the correct symbols to represent modules, parameters, control variables, decisions and repetition.

A structure chart is a representation of the way a system is divided into modules. It provides a hierarchical view of a program by showing major functions at higher levels and the smaller components that make up those functions underneath them. Structure charts are particularly useful when a game contains many different systems that would be difficult to manage as one large program.

A module is a self-contained section of a program that has a particular responsibility. In a game, separate modules might manage player movement, missions, sound, inventory, scoring or menus. Dividing a program into modules is known as modular design. Instead of trying to design and develop the entire game as one piece, developers can work on smaller sections with clearly defined purposes.

A good structure chart begins with the overall system and then breaks it down into major functions. For example, a game might have a main Game module that contains a Menu System, Gameplay System and Save System. The Gameplay System could then be divided into Player Management, Environment Management and Mission Management. The chart therefore shows the relationship between the larger system and its smaller components.

The names used in a structure chart should communicate what each module is responsible for. Names such as "Manage Inventory", "Process Player Input" or "Calculate Results" are more useful than vague names such as "Game Stuff" or "Code". Clear names help developers understand the purpose of each part of the system without needing to inspect the program code.

docs.title: Advantages of Modular Design
docs.text:
• Smaller modules are easier to understand, develop and test.
  • If a problem occurs in one part of the game, developers can investigate the relevant module rather than searching through the entire program.
  • Modules can make it easier for different developers to work on different parts of a project.

docs.title: Game Design Example
docs.text: The following system requires user to validate login details before accessing game menu. Gameplay runs until the game is not running, points earned make their way to game management once players quit back to main menu, which are used to calculate total ongoing score.

docs.title: Structure Charts and DFDs
docs.text:
A structure chart should not be confused with a DFD. A structure chart describes how the program is organised into functional modules, whereas a DFD describes how data moves through a system.

For example, a structure chart might show that a game contains a Player Management module and an Inventory Management module. A DFD could instead show that an Item Pickup process receives an item selection and produces updated inventory data. The two diagrams describe the system from different perspectives.

A school library system allows students to borrow and return books.

  • Students provide their student details and book requests to the library system.

  • If the player has less than 50 energy, the game displays "Not enough energy".

Construct a decision tree that represents the logic used to determine whether the player can perform the special move.

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
A player encounters a locked door.

  • If the player has a key, the door opens.
  • If the player does not have a key, the game checks whether the player has 100 or more coins.
  • If they have 100 or more coins, they can purchase a key and open the door.
  • Otherwise, the door remains locked. *

Construct a decision tree that represents the possible outcomes when the player interacts with the locked door.

Your decision tree should show both decisions and all possible outcomes.

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
A player encounters an enemy in a game.

The game first checks whether the player's health is greater than 0.

  • If the player's health is 0 or less, the player loses the game.
  • If the player is still alive, the game checks whether the enemy's health is greater than 0.
  • If the enemy's health is 0 or less, the player wins the encounter.
  • Otherwise, the game checks whether the player's health is greater than the enemy's health.
    • If it is, the game displays "You have the advantage".
    • Otherwise, the game displays "Enemy has the advantage".

Construct a decision tree that represents the logic used by the game when the player encounters an enemy.

Your decision tree should:

  • Begin with the first condition
  • Show each subsequent decision in the correct order
  • Include every possible branch
  • Include a clear outcome at the end of every branch

docs.title: Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
Learning Intention

  • Develop an efficient computer program by selecting appropriate data types and structures
  • Develop prototypes to communicate design ideas and features to potential end users
  • Implement an event loop in a game or simulation using event-driven programming
  • Simulate a 2D or 3D physical world using fixed time increments
  • Simulate a 2D environment by updating the state of a cell based on its neighbour
  • Modify existing programming code to observe the effects of changing variables
  • Modify existing code to observe changes in an array
  • Identify and correct types of errors, including syntax, logical and run-time
  • Plan and manage a project to create a game and/or simulation using an iterative approach
  • Implement a game or simulation using the preferred design in a general-purpose or object-oriented programming language
  • Develop the UI and UX of a game, including using event-driven programming or an event loop to respond to user input
  • Implement common game features, including the game state
  • Interpret and modify existing programs (code) for games or simulations
  • Design and implement modular programs (code) with functions for games
  • Program selected algorithms and data structures for games or simulations
  • Validate programs using test cases and debug a range of errors
  • Interpret and extend or implement an object-oriented program (code)
  • Test and evaluate the functionality and performance of a simulation or game for specified requirements

Success Criteria

I can follow tutorials to design and construct a platformer game in Unity.

I can implement a range of common game features in Unity.

I can implement a game / simulation using an object-oriented language.

I can document and share my problem solving of specific errors.

I can implement and modify given C# scripts to support a platformer game's functionality.
